sec:
Vote by mail or absentee

Can’t get to your polling place on Election Day? Here is how to vote by mail in Illinois, from the state’s own election office and its laws. Checked October 21, 2026.

Ask for your ballot by

Thursday, October 29Passed

Applications must be in by Thursday, October 29, 2026 (the rule: no less than 5 days before the election; the State Board's Voting by Mail page says requests by mail must be RECEIVED by your election authority by that date). An application delivered in person may be made up to Monday, November 2, 2026 (no less than 1 day before). The State Board urges applying as early as possible. (official page)

Send it back by

Tuesday, November 3Passed

By mail: postmarked on or before Election Day, Tuesday, November 3, 2026, and received by your election authority by Tuesday, November 17, 2026 (within 14 days). In a drop box: by the close of polls, 7 p.m. on November 3, 2026. (official page)

The last day to ask for a ballot by mail has passed. You can still vote in person, early or on Election Day, Tuesday, November 3.You can still vote in person on Election Day, Tuesday, November 3. Early voting in person runs through Monday, November 2, 2026. When and where to vote early.

Ask for a ballot online, on Illinois’s own site

At school away from home, in Illinois or in another state? What Illinois says about students is under Show more.

Who can vote by mail

No reason is needed. Any registered voter can vote by mail in Illinois. Illinois no longer uses the word 'absentee'; a vote-by-mail ballot is the same thing. (official page)

How to ask for a ballot

  • Online. The State Board of Elections' site sends you to your local election authority (your county clerk or city/county election commission): either its online application or a printable form with instructions. Send the application to that local office, not to the State Board. Open it (official page)
  • By mail. Mail the application to your local election authority. A signature is required on a paper application; one made online does not need one. Open it (official page)
  • In person. Apply at your local election authority's office. Open it (official page)

How to send it back

  • By mail. Some election authorities pay the return postage and some do not; your ballot's instructions say which. The Postal Service delivers every ballot even if postage is short, and election offices must accept it. (official page)
  • Drop box. About half of Illinois's election authorities offer secure drop boxes, open until 7 p.m. on Election Day. The State Board lists them. (official page)
  • In person. Deliver it to your election authority's office. Completed mail ballots are NOT accepted at polling places or early voting sites; there you will be offered the choice of giving up the mail ballot and voting in person instead. (official page)
  • Someone else for you. Anyone you choose may deliver your ballot, if you and that person fill out the statement on the ballot envelope about who is delivering it. (official page)

What the envelope needs

Sign the statement (affidavit) on the ballot envelope; it says you voted your own ballot in secret. If someone helps you mark your ballot, their name and address go on the envelope. A candidate may not help you unless they are your spouse, parent, child or sibling. (official page)

Track your ballot

Track your ballot on Illinois’s own site (official page)

Vote early in person instead

Early voting in person is available through Monday, November 2, 2026; your election authority sets the places and hours. (official page)

Students

At school in Illinois, away from home

The state's pages do not speak to students separately. Its general rule: any properly registered Illinois voter may vote by mail, and applications go to the local election authority where you are registered. (official page)

At school in another state, with Illinois as home

The state's pages do not speak separately to students in another state. Its general rule: any properly registered Illinois voter may vote by mail, with the deadlines above. A U.S. citizen temporarily out of the country who keeps a precinct residence in Illinois may also vote by mail. (official page)

Military and overseas

Military voters and their families, and citizens living outside the U.S., can register and request a ballot through Illinois's MOVE site and download the ballot. A request mailed from outside the U.S. that arrives at least 30 days before the election gets a full ballot; one arriving later gets a federal-offices-only ballot. Ballots for these voters go out 45 days before the election. A federal write-in ballot is a backup if yours may not arrive in time. (official page)

Illinois in the Federal Voting Assistance Program’s guide

Good to know

  • Illinois counts a mailed ballot that is postmarked by Election Day and arrives within 14 days, so unofficial results can change for two weeks after Election Day.
  • To check on your ballot, the State Board's FAQ says to contact your election authority; many have status tools on their own websites. The track link goes to the State Board's list of the 108 local election authorities.
  • If your mail ballot is rejected, your election authority must tell you within two days and give you a chance to fix the problem (State Board FAQ).
  • Mail is not always postmarked the day you send it; the State Board suggests asking for a hand postmark at the post office counter when mailing close to Election Day (its 'Who may apply' sheet).
  • If you asked for a mail ballot but want to vote in person, bring it to an early voting site or your polling place to be voided; if you never got it, sign a statement saying so.
  • The State Board's documents differ in detail on one point: its FAQ gives October 29 as the request deadline without separating in-person delivery; its 'Who may apply' sheet says an application delivered in person may be made up to one day before the election.
Where this comes from: 4 pages of Illinois’s election office, its laws and the federal guide
